en: The Ritual Manual of the Earth Goddess Dṛḍhā,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of the Great Nālandā Monastery in Central India by Imperial Decree;
also known as the Sūṣakara Tripiṭaka.
At that time, the Earth Goddess Dṛḍhā and the Great Goddess Mahāśrī both rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,"

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or boys and girls who constantly restrain the five sense faculties and focus their mindfulness with a sincere heart upon me, the Earth Goddess, the Heaven Goddess, and the Goddess of Merit.
To those who prostrate, pay respect, make offerings, and recite my mantra,
I shall constantly bring forth the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) to nourish and sustain them,
causing their lifespan to increase within their bodies.
The vital essence of this earth is overflowing;
within the body of the practitioner,
one attains physical strength, mindfulness, joy, and diligence.
One attains great wisdom and the wealth of eloquence;
one attains the three insights and the six supernormal powers;
one is loved and respected by humans and devas, and attains incomparable and inexhaustible great merit and virtue.
It is like the merit of a noble universal monarch,
such that wherever he travels and wherever he dwells,
it is like the pleasure gardens of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Throughout this life, the next life, and thousands and tens of thousands of births without end,
one shall obtain immense and vast merit,
and receive the devoted service and support of millions of followers day after day.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable beings in states of hardship;
yet [this king] possessed all the necessities of life, with granaries overflowing and the seven treasures in infinite supply,
including the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the wheel-treasure, and the woman-treasure who followed his every wish.
Without being summoned, they come of their own accord, setting limits to birth and death.
To such a bhikṣu who practices the Dharma in this way,
one may provide all manner of gold, silver, precious jewels, various means of livelihood, and all kinds of grain and rice in full abundance.
Thus maintaining mindfulness from the first watch of the night until the middle and latter watches,
whether sitting, lying down, walking, or standing, his mind remains focused on the Dharma without external distractions.
The practitioner may build a monastery, construct a single dwelling, or a grove of trees, or provide clothing, food, bedding, and seats.
He constantly provides the sick with various necessities, such as medicinal decoctions and other requisites for life.
Having obtained these so that they lack nothing,
their bodies attain stability and they are free from sorrow.
With a mind always joyful, one obtains a good field of merit and becomes a vessel for the Dharma.
Having given such gifts,
one shall obtain great rewards in future lives.
With a profound mind that delights in the Dharma, they do not give rise to rebirth in the evil realms nor create unwholesome dharmas.
By protecting such persons in this way, I am able to cultivate a heart of loving-kindness and compassion.
Thus, their various kinds of supreme and wondrous roots of goodness increase and never diminish.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!
This is your heart of diligence;
within the Mahāyāna, it can swiftly increase the power of merit."
At that time, the Earth Deity Dṛḍhā and Śrī-devī addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"For the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness, please proclaim the heart-mantra."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the earth goddess Guṇavatī, saying:
"It is well that you, for the benefit of all sentient beings, wish to proclaim this divine mantra.
Speak it according to your own inclination."
He then spoke the mantra, saying:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ prabhāsvara-ti śrī-samanta āta āta ādu ādu bhr̥ti vibhr̥ti vaye svāhā*. If there is anyone who recites and maintains this mantra for one hundred thousand complete repetitions, [they shall attain success].
This is the foremost dharma.
For those who recite mantras to make offerings to the Earth Deity,
their wealth and nobility shall be limitless, and the seven treasures shall be boundless.
One shall swiftly accomplish all siddhis.
Next, the fundamental body-mudrā is explained:
join the palms and interlace the two index fingers and the two little fingers within the palms.
In the second [mudrā], the two hands are held upright with the backs of the heads touching;
the two thumbs are placed side by side,
pressing against the sides of the two index fingers, which move back and forth.
This accomplishes all activities.
Furthermore, the methods for performing the homa of various accomplishments are explained:
one performs the homa with *śāli* flowers.
One will achieve the fruition of an abundant harvest of the five grains.
Furthermore, by performing homa with *jāti* flowers,
one achieves the fruition of raising a thousand *jin* of silkworms.
Furthermore, there is a method wherein one performs *homa* with non-glutinous rice (*śāli*).
By this, one obtains inexhaustible merit and plants the field of merit for successive lives.
Furthermore, there is a method regarding a place where a single deity resides.
When the multitude gathers at that place,
they perform homa and obtain immense wealth.
Furthermore, there is a method for performing homa with barley and wheat.
One will attain wealth and nobility.
Furthermore, by performing homa with *kaṅkula* grass,
one obtains countless livestock and riches.
Furthermore, there is a method: by performing *homā* with *jāti* flowers before an ancient tomb while residing there,
one becomes greatly wealthy.
Furthermore, there is a method wherein one performs homa with flowers held in the mouth;
this will cause one to be beloved by others.
Furthermore, there is a method for summoning whichever deity of merit one wishes to invoke.
Take twenty-one pieces, each one inch long, from the tail of a blue horse;
recite the mantra during each session of homa,
and the deity of merit will surely come and enter your body.
Furthermore, there is another method:
using green horse dung, empower it twenty-one times with the previously mentioned *bhūmi-devatā* mantra at dawn.
Then, apply it upon the altar, on the doubled person, and on the lintel of a large hearth.
One will immediately obtain wealth according to one's wishes.
Furthermore, there is a method: using the hair from the forehead of a blue horse, perform twenty-one offerings to the deity of merit (*puṇyadevatā*).
The deity of merit will surely be pleased and bestow blessings.

Furthermore, there is a method: take earth from above the lintel of the hearth in a household that possesses merit, and on the eighth day of the twelfth month, bring it to my place and install it there.
One will certainly obtain wealth.
When taking the earth, recite the aforementioned mantra twenty-one times.
This was taught for the upāsaka Sudatta.
The upāsaka Dhanapāla and the upāsikā Puṇyakośaprabhā practiced this dharma.
Furthermore, there was a case where the local spirits were powerful and brought about punishments upon the fourfold assembly;
through the empowerment performed by the aforementioned method, they were cured.
Furthermore, there is a method: take soil from beneath the pestle at a wealthy householder’s home for homa, and one will certainly obtain wealth.
Another method: take soil from within the mouth of a wealthy householder’s grave for homa.
Furthermore, one shall obtain wealth.
The method for painting an image of the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā is as follows:
the male deity is the color of flesh.
Her left hand holds a bowl filled with flowers;
her right palm faces outward.
The female deity is of a white complexion.
The right hand embraces [the image] at the heart;
the left hand embraces it at the thigh.
*Ditian Yigui* (Ritual Manual of Earth and Heaven), one fascicle.
